strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

The current board state is almost entirely empty, with only a single X piece occupying the bottom row of the center column (column 3). As player O, this is effectively the second move of the game. 

In Connect 4 (Connect X with X=4), the center column (3) is the most strategically important due to its role in enabling multiple winning lines (horizontal, vertical, and both diagonals). The opponent has already claimed the bottom spot there. Leaving column 3 open would allow the opponent to immediately play there on their next turn, claiming two consecutive X pieces in the center column and gaining a significant positional advantage for building vertical or diagonal threats.

By dropping in column 3, O claims the next available spot (row 4), preventing the opponent from stacking two X pieces there. This also positions O to control the center column for future development while maintaining flexibility for horizontal or diagonal setups. No immediate threats or blocks are required (no three-in-a-rows exist yet), but this move follows optimal early-game principles by contesting the most valuable column.

Other columns (e.g., 2 or 4) are reasonable alternatives for creating later threats but are suboptimal here, as they cede central control without immediate compensation. Edge columns (0 or 6) are clearly inferior due to limited winning lines.

The current board has a single x in column 3 row 5 (bottom) and an o directly above it in column 3 row 4. Column 3 cannot lead to a vertical win due to alternating parity (would be x-o-x-o-x-o from bottom, preventing 4 in a row). All columns are legal since row 0 is empty everywhere.

Playing in column 2 (or symmetrically column 4) drops an x to row 5 column 2, creating an immediate horizontal two-in-a-row at row 5 columns 2-3 (both x). This forces a win:

- Opponent's response options:
  - Plays column 2 row 5 o: Then play column 5 row 5 x for three-in-a-row (columns 3-5 row 5, all x). Opponent blocks one end next; play the other end for four.
  - Plays column 5 row 5 o: Then play column 2 row 5 x for three-in-a-row (columns 2-4 row 5, all x).
  - Plays column 4 row 4 o (above new x): Then play column 2 row 5 x for three-in-a-row (columns 2-4 row 5, all x).
  - Plays column 3 row 3 o or anywhere else non-adjacent/non-blocking: Then play column 2 row 5 x (or column 5 if playing column 4 first) for immediate three-in-a-row (columns 2-4 row 5, all x).

No opponent move creates a counter-threat (their o is isolated; at best two vertical os, not forcing). Other columns (0,1,5,6) do not connect horizontally to the existing x and offer fewer winning lines. Column 3 stacks uselessly higher without threat.

Columns 2 and 4 are equivalent by symmetry; column 2 chosen as optimal.

Final Answer: 2
